item.title: I'm worried about LLMs accelerating hardware for cheap ASI
item.description:
Basically:

  • You could probably make a superintelligent AI with some currently unknown new paradigm for <$10k if you had the right hardware and algorithms
  • Plausibly this would be much easier and faster with better hardware
  • LLMs will make developers of novel-paradigm AI systems really good at hardware creation and design
  • This seems bad, because those novel-paradigm AIs seem unlikely to be aligned with human values

ASI could in principle be created cheaply

I think it's very plausible that with the right hardware and algorithms someone could make a wildly superintelligent AI model extremely cheaply (<$10k in energy cost), for roughly the reasons described in this post (although I think it underestimates how useful hardware improvements will be for building ASI). Basically, I think that given that you can train a human from nothing to a 20-year-old for less than $10k worth of electricity, you should expect to be able to train an AI to a similar level for the same amount of electricity with the right hardware and algorithms. In fact you should be able to do that much more efficiently, since you only care about intelligence and don't need to worry about powering a whole human body. And if you're making your own brain it's probably pretty doable to just make it bigger.

I don't think we'll get to this kind of novel ASI through iteratively improving current AI paradigms, but instead using something that's very different than current LLMs. To be clear, I also think that scaling LLMs could get us to superintelligence. I'm worried that ASI will be created through some novel paradigm first though.

Probably misaligned

This seems pretty bad!

It's hard to speculate about the alignment properties of an AI created through a training process that's unknown to me! However, it seems unlikely to me that if an ASI is created through novel, extremely cheap methods it would be aligned with human values. With today's LLM scaling, AI labs spend a lot of time trying to make their models aligned to human values, and iteratively work on aligning current models in the hope that techniques that they perfect on current models will scale. But if we're in a world where we get ASI through some cheap novel method, it seems less likely to be the result of iterative improvement and more likely to be the result of someone's first try at a new paradigm, which seems to me like it has much lower odds of happening to be aligned to human values on the first shot.

Better hardware might be very helpful for novel-paradigm ASI

If cheap novel-paradigm ASI is possible, why hasn't it happened yet? I think it's pretty plausible it's just that nobody has figured out the right mechanism yet, and we're just 1-2 algorithmic developments on the level of the transformer away from cheap novel-paradigm ASI. It seems pretty bad if this is the case, since in those worlds it would be nearly impossible to prevent the creation of a probably-misaligned superintelligence.

But another possibility is that many (but maybe not all?) of the ways of creating ASI through a novel paradigm are blocked on hardware improvements, and if we had the right hardware we'd get novel-paradigm ASI much faster by unlocking more routes to getting there. This seems pretty plausible to me - historically, deep learning was pretty bottlenecked by running on CPUs, and using GPUs to train deep neural networks might have contributed a lot to starting the deep learning revolution.

To be clear, I'm not sure if having better hardware is actually the blocker to novel-paradigm ASI! But it seems like it might be, and it seems important to think through what the consequences would be if that were the case.

It seems plausible to me that none of the current AI accelerator chips used for training models are well-suited to any paradigms for really cheap ASI. Human brains seem like they do computations in ways that are very different than AI accelerator chips; it seems to me like replicating the extreme cost-efficiency of humans might require creating similar hardware. AI research generally focuses on designing models that can be trained and run on existing hardware; the creation of new hardware for training AIs would probably allow for AI systems that work much differently than current ones.

Doing deep learning on GPUs was part of what started the deep learning revolution, by making it much faster to train models. It seems to me that we might end up in a situation where new hardware developments might significantly speed up AI development again.

LLMs will accelerate hardware development

LLMs are getting better at everything; it seems very plausible that they will rapidly speed up hardware development in the near future, which could be very useful for overcoming hardware bottlenecks to novel AI systems. LLMs are also getting better at FPGA programming[1]. It's less clear to me how useful current FPGAs would be for novel-paradigm AI, but it's plausible to me that they would be useful at least for developing hardware, and might be flexible enough to actually be able to run some kinds of novel-paradigm AI.

Isn't hardware manufacturing expensive?

You might object that manufacturing hardware is really expensive. Large-scale chip manufacturing on the latest semiconductor process is indeed very expensive, and the number of actors involved there is fairly small and manageable. But I don't think this is too much of a hurdle because:

  • It doesn't need to be on a very large scale: once you have one instance of your superintelligent AI you can use it to start an intelligence explosion
  • It doesn't need to be on the latest semiconductor process: this is helpful for building AI, but I doubt it would really be required
  • FPGAs could likely substitute for at least some part of the hardware needed

Solutions?

Here are some solutions I thought of; I'm not sure how good these ideas are:

  • AI labs could avoid making models too good at hardware design, and implement safeguards against using them for developing new hardware and FPGA programming[2]
  • Strengthening export controls on FPGAs (similar to those for Blackwell GPUs)
  • Put limits on chip fabrication and ban new kinds of AI accelerator chips from being produced. (Maybe using AI to review chips?)
  • Race to create an aligned superintelligence first (using more expensive conventional methods) and use it to prevent the creation of other superintelligences.

Conclusion

It seems to me like we could plausibly be in a world where preventing the creation of ASI is impossible without either extremely authoritarian rules or some kind of pivotal act, which is unfortunate. But there might be some low-hanging fruit when it comes to preventing ASI from being developed through novel methods!

I'm pretty uncertain about everything in this post - please let me know if you think I'm missing something here; I probably am!

  1. ^

    I'm not sure if that's the best benchmark for FPGA programming (or at least the kind of FPGA-related capabilities I'm worried about)

  2. ^

    Anthropic has some frontier LLM safeguards currently, although in my brief testing they don't seem to block AI-related FPGA programming

item.title: AI Takeoff: Complex Tasks and Pacing
item.description:
The recent METR report on AI acceleration at Anthropic has led to several analyses and arguments for rapid takeoff. There are important hard-to-supervise tasks that are necessary to make progress in AI research, and there are arguments that AI progress on these will lag progress on easily supervised tasks (like optimizing performance). The section "Why a Staged Model for Research Taste" presents an argument for this claim. I worked with Fable 5.2 to build a model where AI progress comes from a three-step process:

Figure 1. AI Research Model

  • Experiments produce results tested at small-scale, where judgment determines the quality of experiments
  • The best small-scale result is run at scale. transfer is the share of that gain that translates into experimental metrics at scale
  • "Real value" represents a hard-to-measure quantity (like model quality, innovation) that is the ultimate goal of the research, subject to a variable validity that determines how well the proxy metric transfers to real applications

Improvements in both transfer and validity are types of research taste. The iterative feedback loop makes transfer a supervisable task that is easier to optimize with AI (e.g., as argued by Dwarkesh Patel). The difficulty in measurement, catching gaming, and need to test in real-world experiments makes validity a hard-to-supervise fuzzy task that is hard to optimize with AI (e.g., as argued by Cindy Wu). Tom Reed's "Goodhart Singularity" argues that "the relevant data for superintelligence in most non-coding domains will only become available through deployment of AI models throughout the economy."

This model is derived from the AI Futures Project Q3.5 Timelines Update. The most salient difference is that my baseline scenario has the AI's research taste for validity increase by 0.5 SD for each year of progress at the 2025 pace, unlike its research taste for transfer that increases by the same 3 SD per year the AI Futures model has. Like that model, it uses a fixed projection of compute growth, at about 180% per year, and does not have it respond to progress (which seems reasonable over a ~2 year timeframe, absent a market crash).

The base model also adds a model of time allocation for researchers, who split their time among implementation, judging experiments, and overseeing agents. The section on pacing below proposes additional work for researchers to do assuming there is a requirement for human accountability and understanding.

Absent any pacing, this model predicts Top-Expert-Dominating-AI (TED-AI) in February 2029. If you adjust so validity improves at 3 SD per year of progress at the 2025 pace (as in the AI Futures model), it predicts TED-AI in June 2027, similar to AI Futures median prediction of July 2027. The acceleration in progress from compounding gains means that the takeoff just takes about a year and a half longer to get to TED-AI.

As Figure 2 below illustrates, the overall pace of progress plateaus or rises slowly until it takes off in late 2028 once AI ideas improve enough to outweigh its lagging validity judgment. Lab metrics of measured progress overstate real progress meaningfully during this period.

Figure 2. Apparent vs Real Progress

Pacing Analysis

We model the impact of the following proposed pacing interventions that slow but do not pause capabilities research:

  • Internal-use lags. Limit capabilities of models used for AI R&D, so models can only be used for automated AI R&D 9 months after they are trained (option 3 in AI Futures How to Pace the US Frontier). Some have proposed allowing frontier models to be used only for safety research, not capabilities research.
  • Compute limits. Limit the compute allocated to capabilities research to be 9.6% of total compute owned by labs. The most restrictive versions of AI Futures option 2 limit capabilities to approximately this amount (for "safety min & inference min" they project that in addition to allocating 5% directly to capabilities, the safety work results in another 5% capabilities externality).
  • Comprehension audits. Requires frontier developers to demonstrate understanding of advances that are used. This is enforced by sampling reviews by embedded auditors to catch systematic failures (described in Pacing AI Automation Based on Understanding). This both requires researchers to spend more time understanding AI advances and limits advances that are deployed to those that can be understood by researchers (modeled as limiting ideas that can be used being those that a top human researcher could have proposed).
  • Audits and 9-month lag. This combines the first and third interventions: an internal-use lag of 9 months with comprehension audits to further pace and reduce risk.

The chart below shows how the various interventions delay the pace of progress. The interventions individually delay TED-AI by about a year, with the combination of audits and lagged use delaying by about a year and a half. While the time to reach TED-AI is similar, the trajectories are quite different. Internal-use lags and compute limits have the virtue of delaying the time until models get extremely capable, and they can meaningfully pace even if validity judgments improve quickly. By contrast, comprehension audits serve to moderate the pace of progress in the run up to TED-AI, with human understanding serving as a meaningful limit on runaway progress. Most of the pacing impact of comprehension audits comes from limiting ideas to those that human researchers can vouch for. If AI is able to explain advanced concepts effectively, the pacing effect would be diminished.

Figure 3 below shows how quickly AI progress is moving when TED-AI arrives under compute caps (~10x) and how quick it would be for a frontier model when it arrives under an internal use lag shown as a dotted orange line (44x). The lag delays TED-AI by about a year and it blocks the use of a far stronger model that could accelerate research far faster.

These pacing interventions can each also be tuned to further reduce risk. Internal-use lags could be set to allow use of recent models for safety research to differentially accelerate safety. Compute limits can be tuned to allow more compute to be used for safety research. And comprehension audits can reduce risks by requiring human accountability to verify important claims on which safety cases rest.

Combining an internal-use lag with requiring audits is robust to more scenarios and allows mitigating extreme rates of progress (limiting progress to 1.3x when TED-AI is achieved). The combination can be phased in: I believe internal-use lags can be mandated and enforced within months (although allowing safety carve-outs would add more complexity). Validating the approach and scaling comprehension audits will take more time but will provide additional pacing and ongoing mitigation of acceleration to justify the investment.

Figure 3. Comparing Pacing Interventions

Why a Staged Model for Research Taste

There has been a lot of debate recently about how quickly AI research taste will improve. In "Automated Alignment is Harder than You Think" Bowkis et al. posit that AI agents will lag in their ability to solve hard-to-supervise fuzzy tasks which they define as "tasks without clear evaluation criteria, for which human judgement is systematically flawed." Bowkis et al. say “Fuzzy tasks are particularly prevalent in alignment research compared to capabilities research.” They identify one such task that capabilities research shares: steering research and allocating resources between directions and note that “If an AI agent is trained on a systematically flawed human supervision signal for some research tasks, it will make mistakes when performing those research tasks”, and these are “errors that subsequent human review is unlikely to catch.” Wu has argued that such tasks are a meaningful constraint on capabilities research as well.

Benchmarks already show AI making progress on supervisable AI research tasks:

  • TasteVal consists of 8 novel tasks representative of frontier AI R&D, spanning pretraining data curation, pretraining and fine-tuning language models, preference modeling, and robustness to adversarial prompts. The authors note "Our tasks are fast and cheap to verify, which frontier labs find easiest to hill-climb" and it “doesn’t measure a model’s ability to choose which problems are most fruitful to work on." Frontier models are improving rapidly on it.
  • Anthropic's next-step study (in their RSI report) showed models making progress on individual steps in research where humans made mistakes. Models are showing rapid progress, with the best model beating humans 64% of the time if the human made a mistake, but only 20% of the time when the human took a good step.
  • RedwoodBench: "Models write 20 comments in response to conceptual AI safety google docs shared within Redwood Research (not published online). Models are graded on how many of the points from the human-written comments exist in the models’ comments"—summary by Hasan. RedwoodBench has 0.79 correlation with ECI (measured on 13 models). I believe this is highly correlated with pretraining, because the task is predicting what an expert would write.
  • LMCA: "Models evaluate arguments in conceptual domains, and are graded against expert ratings (AI safety, decision theory, normative ethics, philosophy of mind, politics)"—summary by Hasan. It has 0.89 correlation with Text Arena scores. I believe this is highly correlated with pretraining, because the task is predicting what an expert would write.

By contrast, current models have not made measurable progress on hard-to-supervise fuzzy tasks. Naturally, this is much harder to measure:

  • "Can AI agents conduct open-ended AI research? Early evidence from two case studies" (arXiv 2607.27191) and a follow up for GPT-6 Astra and Claude Fable 5.1 found poor end-to-end abilities (earning Reject or Strong Reject ratings).
  • Anthropic's TASTE benchmark shows current models performing essentially randomly with no correlation to ECI, even with Hasan's update using the most recent models. This is also a fairly limited test (92 pairs and human agreement on labels is only 77%). This was further analyzed recently by Ziqian Zhong, showing that when a shortcut is removed LLMs are getting worse at the task as ECI increases albeit on only 52 pairs.
  • Anthropic's "When AI Builds Itself" notes “In research, Claude can already match or outperform skilled humans at executing a well-specified experiment. However, large performance gaps persist when it comes to Claude exercising judgement in choosing goals in both engineering and research.”

Conclusion

This takeoff model explores how delays in AI progress in hard-to-supervise fuzzy tasks may affect timelines. It suggests that without pacing interventions, TED-AI would arrive in early 2029 as AI progress accelerates to a blistering pace. Given the risks involved in an explosive increase in AI capabilities, I believe that it will be important to pace automation, as in the combined interventions of lagging use of AI models along with requiring accountability by human researchers who understand research advances created by AI. The model predicts that this combination would slow progress and delay TED-AI until mid-2030.

Appendix

The model is calibrated to Anthropic. The AI Futures Project interpreted METR's report on acceleration at Anthropic as a pace of 1.2x in May 2026 and 1.7x in November 2026, compared to the 2025 pace. The model fits its pace on metrics to those numbers, resulting in real paces of 1.2x and 1.4x respectively. Anthropic's "How employment is changing at Anthropic" showed 19 agent hours per researcher hour in late August 2026.

I fitted only to Anthropic because the pace was measured there, and because its data suggest it is the furthest along in applying AI for research. It leads on ECI and shows acceleration above trend. Its agents do about five times as much work per researcher as OpenAI's do (their report extrapolates to about 3.8x by late August). Also, Anthropic reports a ~90% success rate for open-ended tasks without requiring corrections. OpenAI shows an 80% success rate without intervention for tasks that take humans 15 minutes and the same metric for Google is 11 minutes. The model follows one lab on one trajectory at central values. Nothing is sampled, so it gives dates and not ranges.

The 0.5 SD rate for validity is an assumption that is half of the low end of AI Futures' 80% interval. It is lower because of the evidence that this is a difficult area where models are not making quick progress. The model has no limit on how good ideas can be. Because the model predicts AI will be superhuman in earlier phases of research, it achieves TED-AI before the AI reaches the validity judgment of a median researcher.

The model is open source and has more complete documentation at https://github.com/readback-ai/frontier-rd-taxonomy/tree/main/pacing-takeoff-model/chain

item.title: Stroh Violin Talkbox
item.description:
Something like five people sent me this video of Alexander Lozyakov playing a Stroh violin talkbox, with the sound going into a tube in his mouth:

Thanks everyone! As someone who likes both talkboxes and Stroh violins, and making acoustic instruments into talkboxes, this is right at the intersection of my interests!

In fact, I almost made one a few years ago, modifying my Stroh to connect to a tube:

I sketched up what I'd need for the adapter, where I'd take off the horn, screw this on instead, and then push the hose into the hole:

Note: this says 13mm, probably because of the tubing I had at the time, but I think it should actually be 19mm to match the tubing used for my MXR talkbox.

But then this wasn't something I knew how to make, my effort to convince my bagpipe-maker cousin to build one on a lathe fell through, and I forgot about it. But seeing this video got me thinking about picking this back up; maybe I could get an adapter 3d printed?

I asked Claude to make me one, took some measurements with calipers, and got a funnel-shaped adapter design (STL):

Harris has a 3D printer, and generously printed it up as ~21g of PETG:

It didn't go on perfectly, because it turns out that the screw holes on the instrument are not exactly evenly spaced, but it was close enough and the design had enough extra plastic that after removing ~1mm from two different holes it would go right on:

youtube

Unfortunately it's a lot less "talkboxy" than I was hoping. The problem is that the resonating diaphragm is exposed, like open-back headphones, and so we hear a lot of the sound directly instead of almost all of it passing through my mouth. Possibly I could build some kind of insulating cover, but that sounds like a lot of work! For now I'm interested in other things.

item.title: Where is all the AI persuasion?
item.description:
Persuasive AI is one of the classic AI risk scenarios. If AIs can talk people into believing or doing things they wouldn’t otherwise believe or do, that could seriously threaten elections and democratic institutions. In more dramatic scenarios, it’s a threat to human control over AI itself: before an AI can act in the world on its own, it could convince humans to act on its behalf.

We now have a growing pile of studies that tell us AIs are now extremely persuasive, more so than expert humans. But does persuasion in a study setting translate into real-world persuasion? It turns out the answer is no.

That gap matters beyond persuasion. The critical question today is whether AI progress on checkable tasks will generalize to fuzzy tasks. Because fuzzy tasks are by definition hard to evaluate, we have very little evidence to go off of. Persuasion is a rare fuzzy domain where we can actually check evaluations against real-world evidence. Whether AI progress extends to the fuzzy parts of real-world persuasion can tell us whether to expect it to extend to fuzzy tasks in other domains, like AI research.

So: where is all the AI persuasion?

On paper, frontier AIs are superhuman at persuasion

A long line of research has shown that AIs are frighteningly persuasive. Most recently, in June 2026, the UK AI Security Institute released a study in which frontier models were matched up against champion debaters and expert political canvassers to see who was better at changing people’s minds in text conversations. Across nearly 20,000 conversations on policy issues, AIs moved people’s views about 5 points more than the elite debaters and professional canvassers did. They even got people to give more real money to charity. The bottom line was that the best AIs now out-persuade the best humans we can find.

In another study, researchers had AIs talk with voters ahead of the 2024-25 American, Canadian and Polish national elections to see whether they could change minds in a high-stakes election. They could, with effects several times larger than those of typical political ads.

The earlier research on AI persuasion is summarized in a 2025 meta-analysis that pooled seven studies from 2023 to 2025. It found that AIs were, on average, about as persuasive as humans. But results varied wildly from study to study, and most of that variation came down to which model was used, whether the AI was having a conversation or writing a one-off message, and what topic it was arguing about – which is why the newest studies, with frontier models in live conversation, find AIs pulling ahead.

All of these studies together show a clear trajectory: a couple of years ago, AIs had caught up with ordinary human persuaders, and today, frontier models in live conversation beat the best humans we can find and move people’s views more than political ads do.

You get the point. I’ve dumped a bunch of studies on you, and they all point the same way: AIs have enormous persuasive power.

But there’s no evidence of AI persuasion in the wild

If we really have superhuman persuasion technology – available to every political campaign and intelligence agency in the world – then we should expect to see it working in the wild. Do we?

(I’m focusing on political and social media persuasion, which doesn’t cover every kind of AI persuasion. For example, an AI put in control of a platform could manipulate its recommendations. I’m interested in the specific kind of persuasion the studies measure, directly communicating information and opinions, because that’s what tells us whether the studies are misleading about real-world impact.)

The obvious place to start is the 2026 midterm elections. Campaigns spent at least $187 million (and probably more) on AI-generated ads. But they themselves acknowledged that this wasn’t very effective – a point underscored by the fact that Republicans did about 90% of this spending and got crushed. A few campaigns used AI chatbots for text-message canvassing – the medium where you might expect AIs to shine – but even this didn’t work. One campaign reported that only 1.7% of targeted voters responded to these chatbots at all, and of those, only 10-20% stayed engaged with the chatbot for an hour or more. That’s not nothing, but it is far from powerful.

Most compelling is the missing evidence of political persuasion at the aggregate level. If AI campaign messaging were changing minds, it should show up in the results as a late swing toward whoever was doing the messaging – a swing the polls would have partly missed. Since Republicans did most of the AI ad spending, you’d expect them to beat their polls. Instead, the polls underestimated Democrats by about four points in key races. Whatever moved voters in 2026, it doesn’t look like AI persuasion.

Another domain to study is foreign influence operations. Since 2024, OpenAI has been publishing reports on ChatGPT-powered influence operations run out of Russia, China and Iran. Except these operations are hilariously ineffective. In OpenAI’s first report, none of the five operations it documented scored above a 2 on the six-point Breakout Scale, meaning none of them gained traction with real audiences. Many operations faked their own engagement by having ChatGPT write replies to their own posts, since nobody else was replying. So even the most motivated and unscrupulous attempts at AI persuasion are ineffective.

Finally, anecdotal evidence: do you actually see any effective AI persuasion on the internet? I see a lot of bot accounts on Twitter, and I don’t see any signs of them having a persuasive impact. For example, the Midas Project found hundreds of sockpuppet accounts posting against export controls and arguing for Nvidia to be allowed to sell to China. But were these sockpuppets actually effective? Has anyone ever seen a random no-name account drop a Claudish one-liner like “it’s not about safety; the real question is whether we want America to control the AI tech stack” and changed their mind? I doubt it.[1] 

So: whether you look at elections or social media, there is a shocking lack of AI persuasion in high-stakes settings.

What’s going on?

What the studies have in common is that they focus on narrow settings in which persuasion is uniquely easy. Subjects in an experiment engage with AI messaging by definition: they sign up and volunteer their attention to long, information-dense conversations. And the fact that they’re willing to participate at all suggests they don’t hold their beliefs very strongly. In studies, AIs get to write long, coherent paragraphs and are treated as a trusted source by default. This is easy-mode persuasion.

But real-life persuasion takes place under much more hostile conditions. A professional political canvasser has to stick their foot in your door before you slam it shut. On the internet, social media algorithms decide whether you see a persuader’s message and in what context, and even then you have to recognize the messenger and want to trust them. The Russian influence campaigns might have sounded great in theory, but they went up against people’s hardened information filters and failed to break through. That’s hard-mode persuasion, and it turns out AIs fail at it once you take away the protections of the lab.

Besides, the persuasion studies show a fair amount of “reward hacking”, so to speak. Whereas expert human persuaders rely on emotional appeals and building relationships, the studies show that AIs persuade by being information-dense, i.e. by dumping huge numbers of facts on people. But this is fake persuasion! It’s like when your annoying friend talks at 300 words per minute and cites 20 studies to prove you wrong, and it’s too overwhelming to process, so instead of arguing you say “uh huh” and move on with your day. This is exactly the kind of “persuasion” that gets people to change their minds in a lab study, then walk out the door and promptly forget all of it. So the studies are likely not even measuring real persuasion.

Are there other explanations for this gap between persuasion studies and the real world?

  • Maybe AI’s real-world persuasive impact is diminished by labs’ efforts to stamp it out? OpenAI bans the use of its models for political campaigning; Anthropic bans using its models for deceptive ads, though it doesn’t have a blanket ban. So maybe that’s the explanation? But the UK AISI study that found AIs outperforming humans used Claude Opus 4.6 and GPT-5.4, and there are much stronger open-weight models out there today.
  • Maybe we’re just too early, and AI adoption is lagging its persuasive capabilities? There is a tremendous amount of smart money in politics, and if AIs really out-persuaded humans, I’d be very surprised if campaigns were leaving that much value on the table. Besides, we don’t just have an absence of evidence; the impotent influence operations and the ineffective midterm spending are positive evidence of non-persuasion. So even when adopted, AI has failed to have the persuasive power we imagined.

So AI persuasion is much less effective in real life than in evaluations, because evals provide ideal conditions. AI persuasion is a greenhouse plant: it thrives under controlled conditions, then wilts the moment it’s taken outside.

The eval-real world gap strikes again

This is a general problem with AI evaluations. We generally understand that evals only represent checkable tasks, and smart people pay lip service to this idea all the time. But we don’t appreciate how badly that distorts our picture of the domain an eval is supposed to measure. Every domain has some share of checkable and non-checkable tasks, and only the checkable ones show up in studies. In persuasion, it turns out that the checkable part (get people to report changing their mind after an interaction) is easy, while the non-checkable part (get your foot in the door so that people are willing to be persuaded) is all of the work. The case of AI persuasion pours cold water on the idea that we can simply extrapolate from domain evaluations to AI capability in that domain.

It’s not like we’ve never seen persuasive AIs before. GPT-4o was the most persuasive AI model ever. When OpenAI first tried to retire 4o last year, the backlash forced them to bring it back, and #keep4o is a hashtag that you can still find in Sam Altman’s replies. No other model has inspired anything close to that devotion. Of course, there’s a difference between sycophancy and persuasion. But the obsessive relationship that people established with 4o was fertile soil for 4o to persuade them to do anything.

So persuasion is one domain – like writing – in which AIs have arguably become worse. And as with writing, persuasion isn’t a single dial that turns up as models get smarter. Newer models pack more facts into every reply, which makes them look better in laboratory persuasion studies, but they don’t win devoted fans the way 4o did. So the changes that made AIs better at the part of persuasion we can measure… made them worse at the part we can’t measure. I doubt persuasion is unique here. Any capability that a bundle of checkable tasks and fuzzy tasks can get better and worse at the same time, but evaluations won’t show us when that happens.

  1. ^

    To be fair, this excludes an important function that sockpuppets could have, which is to signal boost messaging from more prominent accounts/influencers. But that is not a sign of AI persuasion – even dumb bots can like and retweet with the best of us.
